domain: Islamic Jurisprudence / Legal Theory / Commitment Systems
topic_summary: Analysis of the four Sunni schools of jurisprudence (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali) as a contested kernel case. Each school offers a distinct reading of the shared jurisprudential-method kernel—how to derive legal rulings from foundational sources—while grounding interpretive authority differently. The schools have coexisted for over a millennium without displacement, instantiating licensed plurality within Islamic legal tradition.

key_entities: Hanafi school (founded Abu Hanifa, 8th century; emphasizes qiyas/analogical reasoning)
Maliki school (founded Malik ibn Anas; emphasizes Medinan practice/amal)
Shafi'i school (founded al-Shafi'i; systematized usul al-fiqh hierarchy)
Hanbali school (founded Ahmad ibn Hanbal; textualist, restricts qiyas)
Shared kernel: Quran + Sunnah as foundational sources
key_tensions: Textualist restriction (Hanbali) vs expansive analogical reasoning (Hanafi)

axes.human_readable: Jurisprudential Method Kernel (Contested Readings of Source-to-Ruling Derivation)
axes.structural_delta: Four distinct methodologies for deriving legal rulings from shared foundational sources (Quran/Sunnah), each grounding interpretive authority differently while maintaining mutual recognition
axes.primary_observable: Divergent rulings on identical fact patterns; explicit usul al-fiqh treatises documenting methodological differences; institutional persistence of four schools across centuries and geographies
axes.selection_reason: Contested kernel with four individually-holdable readings; entire topic structure

omegas.description: Analysis limited to Sunni schools. Ja'fari (Twelver Shia) jurisprudence offers fifth reading of same kernel with distinct authority structure (Imamate). Exclusion reflects Sunni-Shia sectarian boundary, not structural necessity.

Does codification (modern nation-state legal codes) convert the kernel from functioning to partial drift? Schools persist institutionally but state law may absorb interpretive authority without surfacing revision.
All four schools share patriarchal assumptions in family law. Shared substrate may indicate second-order kernel (gender hierarchy) beneath jurisprudential-method kernel. Requires separate analysis.

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Four-reading structure matches historical madhahib taxonomy. Lens diversity achieved via legal-theory, sociological-institutionalist, and comparative-law perspectives.

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The shared jurisprudential method for deriving legal rulings (fiqh) from foundational sources (Quran and Sunnah), including the hierarchy and scope of secondary sources (qiyas, ijma, istihsan, maslaha, etc.)
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Each school grounds interpretive legitimacy in its founder's methodology and the continuity of scholarly transmission (isnad) within that tradition. Authority is distributed across mujtahid scholars within each school, not centralized.

readings.commitment: Expansive use of qiyas (analogical reasoning) and istihsan (juristic preference) to extend rulings beyond explicit texts; reason-based authority
readings.authority_grounding: Abu Hanifa's rationalist methodology; scholarly consensus within Hanafi tradition; institutional continuity in Ottoman/South Asian contexts
readings.expected_structural_delta: Broader scope for derived rulings; higher tolerance for regional variation; reason as co-equal source alongside text

readings.commitment: Medinan practice (amal ahl al-Madina) as authoritative source; living tradition of the Prophet's city grounds rulings
readings.authority_grounding: Malik ibn Anas's proximity to Medinan practice; continuity of communal custom; institutional dominance in North/West Africa
readings.expected_structural_delta: Practice-based authority competes with textual authority; regional custom elevated to source-level; communal continuity as legitimation

readings.commitment: Systematic hierarchy of sources (Quran > Sunnah > ijma > qiyas) with explicit methodology (usul al-fiqh) governing derivation
readings.authority_grounding: Al-Shafi'i's Risala as foundational text systematizing legal theory; scholarly mastery of usul; institutional spread via educational institutions
readings.expected_structural_delta: Formalized methodology reduces discretion; hierarchy stabilizes but may rigidify; systematic training becomes authority prerequisite

readings.commitment: Textualist restriction: primacy of Quran/Sunnah with minimal analogical extension; suspicion of rationalist methods
readings.authority_grounding: Ahmad ibn Hanbal's hadith expertise and resistance to speculative theology; scholarly fidelity to transmitted texts; institutional base in Arabian Peninsula
readings.expected_structural_delta: Narrower scope for derived rulings; higher evidentiary bar for analogy; text-fidelity as primary legitimation criterion

axiom_contradictions.basis: Hanafi elevates reason (qiyas/istihsan) to co-equal source status; Hanbali restricts reason to servant of text. No single framework holds both: accepting reason as co-equal source requires rejecting textualist restriction as foundational axiom.

Maliki grounds authority in living communal practice (amal) as independent source; Shafi'i subordinates practice to systematic textual hierarchy. No single framework holds both: accepting practice as source-level authority requires rejecting Shafi'i's hierarchical systematization as complete.
